{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q1070228]] Wikidata name: Lingyin Temple [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:51, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Use American English|date=April 2023}} {{Use mdy dates|date=April 2023}} {{Short description|Buddhist temple in Hangzhou, China}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Lingyin temple | native_name = 灵隐寺 | native_name_lang = zh | image = Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou 20161003.jpg | caption = [[:en:Hall of Bhaisajyaguru|Hall of Bhaisajyaguru]] in the Temple | map_type = Zhejiang#China | map_caption = | coordinates = {{coord|30.2427777778|N|120.096666667|E|type:landmark_region:China|format=dms|display=title,inline}} | coordinates_footnotes = | religious_affiliation = [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] | sect = [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhism]] | leadership = Shi Guangquan ({{zh|s=释光泉|t=|labels=no}}) | festival = | location = [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]], [[:en:Zhejiang|Zhejiang]] | country = China | consecration_year = | website = {{URL|http://www.lingyinsi.org/}} | architect = | architecture_type = | architecture_style = [[:en:Chinese architecture|Chinese architecture]] | founded_by = [[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]] | creator = | funded_by = | general_contractor = | established = 328 | groundbreaking = | year_completed = [[:en:Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]] (reconstruction) | construction_cost = | date_demolished = | footnotes = }} [[File:West Lake Map.png|thumb|Map of the West Lake in Hangzhou, China, with the location of Lingyin Temple]] [[File:Chanting at Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou.ogg|thumb|Buddhist monks chanting at Lingyin Temple, [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]], October 2010.]]
'''Lingyin Temple''' ({{zh|t=靈隱寺|s=灵隐寺|p=Língyǐn Sì}}) is a prominent [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhist]] temple near [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]] that is renowned for its many pagodas and grottos.{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=85}} Its name is commonly and literally translated into English as '''Temple of the Soul's Retreat'''.
The monastery is the largest of several temples in the Wulin Mountains ({{zh|c=武林山|p=Wǔlínshān}}), which feature renowned grottos and religious rock carvings.
==History== According to tradition, the monastery was founded in 328 AD during the [[:en:Eastern Jin dynasty|Eastern Jin dynasty]] (266–420) by an Indian monk, named [[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]] in Chinese. From its inception, Lingyin was a famous monastery in the [[:en:Jiangnan|Jiangnan]] region.{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=85}} At its peak under the [[:en:Wuyue|Wuyue]] Kingdom (907–978), the temple boasted 18 pavilions, 72 halls, more than 1300 dormitory rooms, inhabited by more than 3000 monks. Many of the rich Buddhist carvings in the Feilai Feng grottos and surrounding mountains also date from this era.
During the [[:en:Southern Song Dynasty|Southern Song]] (1127–1279), the monastery was regarded as one of the ten most important temples of the Chan sect in the [[:en:Jiangnan|Jiangnan]] region. However, its prominence has not saved the temple from marauders. It has been rebuilt no less than sixteen times since then. While certain existing buildings date from previous Chinese dynasties, much of the current buildings are modern restorations from the late [[:en:Qing dynasty|Qing]] (1644–1911) period.
During the [[:en:Cultural Revolution|Cultural Revolution]], the temple and grounds suffered damage at the hands of [[:en:Red Guards (China)|red guards]], but the students of [[:en:Zhejiang University|Zhejiang University]] tried to protect the temple. The temple managed to avoid large scale destruction partly because of the instructions of Premier [[:en:Zhou Enlai|Zhou Enlai]].
Today the temple is thriving as a destination for both pilgrims and tourists. It is regarded as one of the wealthiest monasteries in China, and regular pilgrims have included former paramount leader [[:en:Deng Xiaoping|Deng Xiaoping]].
==Surroundings== The Wuling Mountains are a renowned site for [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhism]] in Southern China. A number of smaller temples are also located in the area. Today, Lingyin and the surrounding areas are marketed as the Lingyin-Feilai Feng Scenic Area, with ticketed admission. Visitors enter from a screen wall marked with a four character inscription "the Western Heaven is within reach" ({{zh|t=咫尺西天|p=zhíchǐ Xītiān|l=Western Heaven is between 0.8 and one foot away|labels=no}}). Proceeding down the road from the entrance, the visitor first sees Feilai Feng on the left, then Lingyin Hill on the right. The entire scenic area is dotted with historic buildings and artwork, including pagodas, pavilions, bridges, and statues. The largest stone pagoda is located near the entrance. Called Elder Li's Pagoda ({{zh|t=理公塔}}), it houses the ashes of Huili. The area is thickly wooded.
==Feilai Feng grottos== [[File:LigongPagoda.jpg|thumb|left|Pagoda containing [[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]]'s ashes at the foot of Feilai Feng.|300x300px]] [[File:Lingyin grotto.JPG|thumb|right|[[:en:Rock reliefs|Rock reliefs]] at Feilai Feng; the panel at lower left depicts the pilgrims of the ''[[:en:Journey to the West|Journey to the West]]''|188x188px]] [[File:Maitreya and disciples carving in Feilai Feng Caves.jpg|thumb|Relief of [[:en:Budai|Budai]] as [[Maitreya]], with disciples]] Feilai Feng, or "the Peak that Flew Hither", also commonly translated as "Flying Peak" ([[:en:Traditional Chinese characters|Traditional Chinese]]: 飛來峰石窟; [[:en:Simplified Chinese characters|Simplified Chinese]]:飞来峰石窟), is located in front of the temple proper. The peak is so-named because it is made of limestone, giving it a craggy appearance very different from the surrounding mountains. Legend holds that the peak was originally from [[:en:India|India]] (with some versions suggesting that it is [[:en:Vulture Peak|Vulture Peak]]), but flew to [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]] overnight as a demonstration of the omnipotence of Buddhist law. Many grottos can be found on the peak, such as Qinglin Grotto, Yuru Grotto and Longhong Grotto. Many [[:en:rock relief|rock relief]]s dot the peak surface, and more are located in the various caves and grottos throughout the peak. Within the main cave, dedicated to the [[:en:Bodhisattva|Bodhisattva]] [[Kannon|Guanyin]], there is a crack in the ceiling of the cave that stretches up to the surface, so that a person standing at a certain position can see a sliver of sunlight. This is known as the "one thread of heaven" ([[:en:Traditional Chinese characters|Traditional Chinese]]: 一線天; [[:en:Simplified Chinese characters|Simplified Chinese]]: 一线天; [[:en:Pinyin|Pinyin]]: ''Yīxiàn Tiān'').{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=86–87}}
The stone carvings on Feilai Feng are located in an area measuring 600 meters long and 200 meters wide. In total, there are 153 shrines and more than 470 pieces of carvings, among which 338 are relatively well-preserved, 96 carvings from the [[:en:Yuan dynasty|Yuan Dynasty]] as well as several from the [[:en:Ming dynasty|Ming Dynasty]].
Around 11 carvings date to the late [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and [[:en:Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period|Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period]]. These carvings dot the top of the peak and the mouth of Qinglin Grotto and they all prominently feature the “Three Saints of the West”, which refers to the triad of [[Amitābha]] Buddha and the Bodhisattvas [[Kannon|Guanyin]] and [[:en:Mahasthamaprapta|Mahasthamaprapta]] from [[:en:Pure Land Buddhism|Pure Land Buddhism]].
A total of 222 carvings were produced in the [[:en:Song dynasty|Northern Song Dynasty]] period, which feature a diverse range of Buddhist figures including the Six Patriarchs of [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan]] (or [[:en:Zen|Zen]]) Buddhism, various arhats, Bodhisattvas and Buddhas such as [[:en:Vairocana|Vairocana]]. One of the more prominent carvings from this period is a shrine to [[:en:Budai|Budai]], a monk who is traditionally regarded as an incarnation of [[Maitreya]], surrounded by the [[:en:Eighteen Arhats|Eighteen Arhats]]. This shrine stands at 3.6 meters high and 9.9 meters long, making it the largest shrine on Feilai Feng.
Most of the nearly 100 carvings produced during the Yuan Dynasty are located on the southern bank of Lengquan Stream and on the cliff near Qinglin Grotto and Yuru Grotto. The carvings from this period resembles the art styles of the [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang]] and [[:en:Song dynasty|Song]] dynasties, while also reflecting influences from [[:en:Tibetan Buddhism|Tibetan]] and [[:en:Mongolia|Mongolia]]n art.
==Architecture== [[File:杭州 灵隐寺 - panoramio (1).jpg|thumb|250x250px|[[:en:Shanmen|Shanmen]] of the temple]] The main axis of Lingyin follows a traditional Song dynasty five-hall Chan sect structure. The main axis stretches up the Lingyin Hill. However, the five-hall axis is a recent recreation. Only the front three halls are a part of the [[:en:Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]] axis.
===Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings=== The formal entrance of the temple is the [[:en:Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings|Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings]]. This hall is a double-eaved building. The front of the building carries a plaque ({{zh|p=Yúnlín Chán Sì|l=[[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan]] temple of the Clouds and Forests|labels=no|t=雲林禪寺}}), written by the [[:en:Kangxi Emperor|Kangxi Emperor]]. The principal statue in this hall is that of the [[Maitreya]] Buddha in his manifestation as [[:en:Budai|Budai]], or the [[:en:Laughing Buddha|Laughing Buddha]]. At the back, facing up the hill, is the [[:en:Skanda (Buddhism)|Skanda]] Buddha, or Weituo as he is known in Chinese. This statue dates from the [[:en:Southern Song Dynasty|Southern Song Dynasty]]. Being 800 years old this is the oldest and most important statue in the temple. Arranged along the left and right are the [[Four Heavenly Kings]]. The ceiling is ornately painted and decorated with [[:en:Fenghuang|phoenixes]] and [[:en:Chinese dragon|dragons]].{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=86}}
The statues of [[Four Heavenly Kings]] are imposing. Visitors to the temple are often impressed by the size and majesty of the entrance hall and its statues of the heavenly kings. Indeed, the hall of the Heavenly Kings at the Lingyin Temple is as large or larger than the main hall at many temples, reflecting its status as the center of Buddhism in Southern China.
The Hall of the Heavenly Kings is the formal entrance to the temple. However, this entry has been closed in recent years, with visitors funneled instead through side doors, where separate ticket offices are set up for admission to the temple.
===Mahavira Hall=== [[File:Hangzhou Lingyin-Temple 20161003.jpg|thumb|248x248px|The [[:en:Mahavira Hall|Mahavira Hall]]]] The second and principal hall is the [[:en:Mahavira Hall|Mahavira Hall]] (also referred to as the Grand Hall of the Great Sage). It is separated from the Hall of the Heavenly Kings by a large courtyard, featuring a raised lawn bordered with trees. To the left of the courtyard stands the [[#Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]]. The Mahavira Hall stands at 33.6 meters tall and has a roof that is triple-eaved. The interior of the hall reaches about 30 meters, with a gold-painted ceiling featuring bas-relief images of traditional Buddhist symbols.{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=86–87}}
[[File:Lingyin Buddha.JPG|thumb|The [[Shakyamuni]] Buddha statue at the [[:en:Mahavira Hall|Mahavira Hall]].]] The main statue enshrined within this hall is one of [[Shakyamuni|Sakyamuni]], the historical [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]], with his right hand forming the [[:en:Vitarka Mudrā|vitarka mudrā]]. The present statue was carved in 1956 from [[:en:Camphor|Camphor]] wood in [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang dynasty]] style and coated with 60 [[:en:Tael|Tael]]s of gold. At 24.6 meters high (including the throne on which the statue sits), it is the largest wooden Buddhist statue in China. Arranged along each side of the hall are statues of the [[:en:Twenty-Four Protective Deities|Twenty-Four protective deities]] of Chinese Buddhism, their hands carrying various Buddhist instruments of salvation as well as weapons. Statues of the [[:en:Eighteen Arhats|Eighteen arhats]] and other prominent Buddhist figures, such as the Bodhisattva [[:en:Cundi (Buddhism)|Cundi]], line the walls of the hall as well.
Behind the hall are twelve statues of various different bodhisattvas lining each wall, with six of each side. The statues include those of [[Manjushri|Manjusri]], [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]], [[Maitreya]] and [[Vajragarbha]].
, a manifestation of the Bodhisattva [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Avalokiteśvara]], at the back of the Mahavira Hall|273x273px]] At the rear wall of the hall is a [[:en:panorama|panorama]] depicting the penultimate chapter of the [[:en:Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra]], centering on [[:en:Sudhana|Sudhana]] ({{zh|t=善財童子|p=Shàncáitóngzǐ}}). In the chapter, Sudhana, in pursuit of enlightenment, goes on a pilgrimage to 53 different spiritual teachers (ranging from non-Buddhists to Bhikkhunīs to kings to devas to Bodhisattvas). The central statue of the panorama is one of the Bodhisattva [[Kannon|Guanyin]] (one of the 53 teachers). Statues of Sudhana and [[:en:en:Longnü|en:Longnü]] stand at both sides of this statue. The rest of the panorama behind the three main statues consists of more than 150 clay sculptures depicting the other spiritual teachers of Sudhana as well as other Buddhist figures such the main characters of [[:en:Journey to the West|Journey to the West]], the [[Four Heavenly Kings]] and [[:en:Ji Gong|Ji Gong]]. Figures of the Bodhisattva [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Ksitigarbha]] and [[Shakyamuni|Sakyamuni]] Buddha (depicting his cultivation prior to becoming the Buddha) are also incorporated into the top and middle portions of the panorama respectively.
===Hall of Bhaisajyaguru=== Further uphill and behind the main hall is the [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Hall of Bhaisajyaguru]] ({{zh|p=Yàoshī Diàn|labels=no|t=藥師殿}}), housing a statue of the [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Bhaisajyaguru]] Buddha, commonly called the Medicine Buddha. Statues of the Bodhisattvas [[:en:Sūryaprabha|Sūryaprabha]] and [[:en:Candraprabha|Candraprabha]], who are traditionally regarded as the attendants of Bhaisajyaguru, stand on the left and right side of Bhaisajyaguru's statue respectively.
Twelve statues of the [[Twelve Heavenly Generals]], who are protective [[:en:Yaksha|Yaksha]] attendants of [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Bhaisajyaguru]], stand on both sides of the Hall of Bhaisajyaguru, with 6 situated on each side. The names of each General along with their associated iconography are: Kumbhira (armed with a yellow vajra), Vajra (armed with a white sword), Mihira (armed with a yellow vajra), Andira (armed with a green mallet), Anila (armed with a red trident), Sandila (armed with a black sword), Indra (armed with a red staff or halberd), Pajra (armed with a red mallet), Makura (armed with a white ax), Kinnara (armed with a yellow rope), Catura (armed with a green mallet), and Vikarala (armed with a red three-pointed vajra).
=== Hall of Ji Gong === [[File:Lingyin Temple, 2020-11-29 16.jpg|thumb|246x246px|The Hall of [[:en:Ji Gong|Ji Gong]]]] This hall is situated to the east of the Hall of Bhaisajyaguru and enshrines a statue of the Song dynasty monk [[:en:Ji Gong|Ji Gong]] (also known as "Daoji"). The statue is made of bronze, with a height of 2.3 meters and a weight of 2.5 tons. The right hand of the statue holds a broken fan, the left hand carries Buddhist prayer beads, and the right foot is shown dipping into a wine jar. Eighteen huge murals depicting a narration of Ji Gong’s life are painted on the walls at both sides of the hall. Each mural is 3 meters high and 3 meters long, with the entire display being 50 meter long.
===Dharma Hall=== [[File:Hangzhou-Lingyin-Tempel-52-Teich-Pavillons-2012-gje.jpg|thumb|249x249px|[[:en:Free Life Pond|Free Life Pond]] of the temple]] The [[:en:Dharma Hall|Dharma Hall]] is located behind the Hall of Bhaisajyaguru and is the main place where the Buddhist sutras are expounded by the resident monastics. The present Dharma Hall building was constructed by a monk from the temple named Xuanli in 1446.
=== Cultural Relics Exhibition Hall === The Cultural Relics Exhibition Hall lies on the basement floor of the Dharma Hall and displays the collection of Buddhist cultural relics maintained by the temple.
The hall covers a total area of 638 square meters and is installed with waterproof, fireproof, damp-proof, electronic surveillance and air-conditioning systems. It houses an exhibition of over 40 showcases with collections of cultural relics that have been treasured by the temple for many years. These cultural relics are categorized by the temple into four categories: first, Buddhist ritual implements used by successive abbots of Lingyin Temple, such as horsetail whisks and [[:en:Ruyi (scepter)|ruyi scepters]]; second, common antiques such as porcelain vases from the Southern Song Dynasty; third, Buddhist antiques such as sutras written by Tang dynasty Chinese Buddhists and unearthed Buddhist statues; fourth, ancient paintings and calligraphy, such as calligraphy scrolls in seal characters by [[:en:Wu Changshuo|Wu Changshuo]], fan paintings by [[:en:Ren Bonian|Ren Bonian]] and couplets by [[:en:Sha Menghai|Sha Menghai]].
=== Buddhist Texts Library === Uphill from the Hall of the Medicine Buddha is the [[:en:Buddhist Texts Library|Buddhist Texts Library]]. This, and the Huayan Hall behind it, were built from 2000 to 2002 to recreate the five-hall main axis. The Sutra Library does not house a major statue and is not open for worship.
===Huayan Hall=== The fifth and last hall on the main axis is the Avatamsaka Hall, or Huayan Hall ({{zh|c=华严殿|p=Huáyán Diàn|labels=no}}). Also built in 2002, this hall houses statues of the three sages of the [[:en:Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra]], known as the Huayan Sutra in [[:en:Chinese language|Chinese]] – [[Shakyamuni|Sakyamuni]], [[:en:Manjusri|Manjusri]], and [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]].
A 3 meter high bronze statue of the Japanese Buddhist monk [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]], who traveled to China during the Tang Dynasty to study [[:en:Chinese Esoteric Buddhism|Chinese Esoteric Buddhism]] and who visited Lingyin Temple during his travels, stands in a bamboo grove between the Dharma Hall and the Huayan Hall. The statue portrays Kūkai in monastic robes, holding Buddhist prayer beads in his left hand, and a walking stick in his right hand. The statue was erected in 2002 as a symbol of the friendship between Buddhist circles in both China and Japan.
===Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats=== The Hall of Five Hundred Arhats ({{zh|t=五百羅漢堂|p=Wǔbǎi Luóhàn Táng|labels=no}}), also a modern addition, faces onto the western side of the courtyard in front of the main hall. The building has a complex floor plan, shaped like a Buddhist [[:en:Swastika|Swastika]]. Bronze statues of the five hundred arhats are arranged along the arms of the swastika, with each statue seated on a unique ornate seat. Each statue measures 1.7 meters in height, 1.3 meters in width, and weighs around 1 ton.
At the center of the hall, where the arms of the swastika join, stands a bronze canopy housing statues of the four main bodhisattvas in Chinese Buddhism: [[Kannon|Guanyin]], [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Ksitigarbha]], [[Manjushri|Manjusri]] and [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]], who represent the four cardinal directions. This canopy is 12.62 meters in height, 7.77 meters wide and occupies 5 square meters. It is currently the tallest solid bronze structure in the world.
=== Two Sutra Pillars === The two sutra pillars are located in the eastern and western sides of the Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings. The eastern pillar stands at 7.17 meters high and the western pillar stands at 11 meters high. Both pillars are engraved with the [[:en:Uṣṇīṣa Vijaya Dhāraṇī Sūtra|Uṣṇīṣa Vijaya Dhāraṇī Sūtra]], as well as reliefs of various Buddhist figures and tales. Both pillars were built in the year 969 in the state of [[:en:Wuyue|Wuyue]] during the end of the [[:en:Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period|Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period]] and the beginning of the [[:en:Song dynasty|Song Dynasty]] and were moved to their present location in the temple in the year 1053.
==Notable monks== *[[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]] - An Indian monk who founded the temple *[[:en:Ji Gong|Daoji]] – A saintly Buddhist monk who is highly venerated in [[:en:Chinese folk religion|Chinese folk religion]] and popularly known as "Ji Gong". *Dachuan Lingyin Puji (1179–1253)- compiler of the Wudeng Huiyan (''Compendium of Five Lamps'')

Hangzhou, China Part 1.jpg|Statues of the [[:en:Twenty-Four Protective Deities|Twenty-Four Devas]] (二十四諸天 ''Èrshísì Zhūtiān'') on the right side of the Mahavira Hall File:Xihu, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China - panoramio (32).jpg|Arhat statues enshrined inside the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:杭州.灵隐寺（五百罗汉堂） - panoramio (1).jpg|Statue of [[Manjushri|Manjusri]] in the Bronze Canopy within the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:杭州.灵隐寺（五百罗汉堂） - panoramio (2).jpg|Statue of [[Kannon|Guanyin]] in the Bronze Canopy within the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:杭州.灵隐寺（五百罗汉堂） - panoramio (3).jpg|Statue of [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Ksitigarbha]] in the Bronze Canopy within the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:杭州.灵隐寺（五百罗汉堂） - panoramio (4).jpg|Statue of [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]] in the Bronze Canopy within the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:2013.1灵隐0154.JPG|Rock carving of [[:en:Budai|Budai]] in the grottos File:Lingyin Temple 20150623 100717.jpg|Statues in the grottos File:Lingyin temple 03.jpg|Statues in the grottos File:Hangzhou-Lingyin-Tempel-60-Buddha-Grotten-2012-gje.jpg|Statues in the grottos </gallery>

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q1070228]] Wikidata name: Lingyin Temple [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:51, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Use American English|date=April 2023}} {{Use mdy dates|date=April 2023}} {{Short description|Buddhist temple in Hangzhou, China}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Lingyin temple | native_name = 灵隐寺 | native_name_lang = zh | image = Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou 20161003.jpg | caption = [[:en:Hall of Bhaisajyaguru|Hall of Bhaisajyaguru]] in the Temple | map_type = Zhejiang#China | map_caption = | coordinates = {{coord|30.2427777778|N|120.096666667|E|type:landmark_region:China|format=dms|display=title,inline}} | coordinates_footnotes = | religious_affiliation = [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] | sect = [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhism]] | leadership = Shi Guangquan ({{zh|s=释光泉|t=|labels=no}}) | festival = | location = [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]], [[:en:Zhejiang|Zhejiang]] | country = China | consecration_year = | website = {{URL|http://www.lingyinsi.org/}} | architect = | architecture_type = | architecture_style = [[:en:Chinese architecture|Chinese architecture]] | founded_by = [[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]] | creator = | funded_by = | general_contractor = | established = 328 | groundbreaking = | year_completed = [[:en:Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]] (reconstruction) | construction_cost = | date_demolished = | footnotes = }} [[File:West Lake Map.png|thumb|Map of the West Lake in Hangzhou, China, with the location of Lingyin Temple]] [[File:Chanting at Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou.ogg|thumb|Buddhist monks chanting at Lingyin Temple, [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]], October 2010.]]
'''Lingyin Temple''' ({{zh|t=靈隱寺|s=灵隐寺|p=Língyǐn Sì}}) is a prominent [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhist]] temple near [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]] that is renowned for its many pagodas and grottos.{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=85}} Its name is commonly and literally translated into English as '''Temple of the Soul's Retreat'''.
The monastery is the largest of several temples in the Wulin Mountains ({{zh|c=武林山|p=Wǔlínshān}}), which feature renowned grottos and religious rock carvings.
==History== According to tradition, the monastery was founded in 328 AD during the [[:en:Eastern Jin dynasty|Eastern Jin dynasty]] (266–420) by an Indian monk, named [[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]] in Chinese. From its inception, Lingyin was a famous monastery in the [[:en:Jiangnan|Jiangnan]] region.{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=85}} At its peak under the [[:en:Wuyue|Wuyue]] Kingdom (907–978), the temple boasted 18 pavilions, 72 halls, more than 1300 dormitory rooms, inhabited by more than 3000 monks. Many of the rich Buddhist carvings in the Feilai Feng grottos and surrounding mountains also date from this era.
During the [[:en:Southern Song Dynasty|Southern Song]] (1127–1279), the monastery was regarded as one of the ten most important temples of the Chan sect in the [[:en:Jiangnan|Jiangnan]] region. However, its prominence has not saved the temple from marauders. It has been rebuilt no less than sixteen times since then. While certain existing buildings date from previous Chinese dynasties, much of the current buildings are modern restorations from the late [[:en:Qing dynasty|Qing]] (1644–1911) period.
During the [[:en:Cultural Revolution|Cultural Revolution]], the temple and grounds suffered damage at the hands of [[:en:Red Guards (China)|red guards]], but the students of [[:en:Zhejiang University|Zhejiang University]] tried to protect the temple. The temple managed to avoid large scale destruction partly because of the instructions of Premier [[:en:Zhou Enlai|Zhou Enlai]].
Today the temple is thriving as a destination for both pilgrims and tourists. It is regarded as one of the wealthiest monasteries in China, and regular pilgrims have included former paramount leader [[:en:Deng Xiaoping|Deng Xiaoping]].
==Surroundings== The Wuling Mountains are a renowned site for [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhism]] in Southern China. A number of smaller temples are also located in the area. Today, Lingyin and the surrounding areas are marketed as the Lingyin-Feilai Feng Scenic Area, with ticketed admission. Visitors enter from a screen wall marked with a four character inscription "the Western Heaven is within reach" ({{zh|t=咫尺西天|p=zhíchǐ Xītiān|l=Western Heaven is between 0.8 and one foot away|labels=no}}). Proceeding down the road from the entrance, the visitor first sees Feilai Feng on the left, then Lingyin Hill on the right. The entire scenic area is dotted with historic buildings and artwork, including pagodas, pavilions, bridges, and statues. The largest stone pagoda is located near the entrance. Called Elder Li's Pagoda ({{zh|t=理公塔}}), it houses the ashes of Huili. The area is thickly wooded.
==Feilai Feng grottos== [[File:LigongPagoda.jpg|thumb|left|Pagoda containing [[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]]'s ashes at the foot of Feilai Feng.|300x300px]] [[File:Lingyin grotto.JPG|thumb|right|[[:en:Rock reliefs|Rock reliefs]] at Feilai Feng; the panel at lower left depicts the pilgrims of the ''[[:en:Journey to the West|Journey to the West]]''|188x188px]] [[File:Maitreya and disciples carving in Feilai Feng Caves.jpg|thumb|Relief of [[:en:Budai|Budai]] as [[Maitreya]], with disciples]] Feilai Feng, or "the Peak that Flew Hither", also commonly translated as "Flying Peak" ([[:en:Traditional Chinese characters|Traditional Chinese]]: 飛來峰石窟; [[:en:Simplified Chinese characters|Simplified Chinese]]:飞来峰石窟), is located in front of the temple proper. The peak is so-named because it is made of limestone, giving it a craggy appearance very different from the surrounding mountains. Legend holds that the peak was originally from [[:en:India|India]] (with some versions suggesting that it is [[:en:Vulture Peak|Vulture Peak]]), but flew to [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]] overnight as a demonstration of the omnipotence of Buddhist law. Many grottos can be found on the peak, such as Qinglin Grotto, Yuru Grotto and Longhong Grotto. Many [[:en:rock relief|rock relief]]s dot the peak surface, and more are located in the various caves and grottos throughout the peak. Within the main cave, dedicated to the [[:en:Bodhisattva|Bodhisattva]] [[Kannon|Guanyin]], there is a crack in the ceiling of the cave that stretches up to the surface, so that a person standing at a certain position can see a sliver of sunlight. This is known as the "one thread of heaven" ([[:en:Traditional Chinese characters|Traditional Chinese]]: 一線天; [[:en:Simplified Chinese characters|Simplified Chinese]]: 一线天; [[:en:Pinyin|Pinyin]]: ''Yīxiàn Tiān'').{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=86–87}}
The stone carvings on Feilai Feng are located in an area measuring 600 meters long and 200 meters wide. In total, there are 153 shrines and more than 470 pieces of carvings, among which 338 are relatively well-preserved, 96 carvings from the [[:en:Yuan dynasty|Yuan Dynasty]] as well as several from the [[:en:Ming dynasty|Ming Dynasty]].
Around 11 carvings date to the late [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and [[:en:Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period|Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period]]. These carvings dot the top of the peak and the mouth of Qinglin Grotto and they all prominently feature the “Three Saints of the West”, which refers to the triad of [[Amitābha]] Buddha and the Bodhisattvas [[Kannon|Guanyin]] and [[:en:Mahasthamaprapta|Mahasthamaprapta]] from [[:en:Pure Land Buddhism|Pure Land Buddhism]].
A total of 222 carvings were produced in the [[:en:Song dynasty|Northern Song Dynasty]] period, which feature a diverse range of Buddhist figures including the Six Patriarchs of [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan]] (or [[:en:Zen|Zen]]) Buddhism, various arhats, Bodhisattvas and Buddhas such as [[:en:Vairocana|Vairocana]]. One of the more prominent carvings from this period is a shrine to [[:en:Budai|Budai]], a monk who is traditionally regarded as an incarnation of [[Maitreya]], surrounded by the [[:en:Eighteen Arhats|Eighteen Arhats]]. This shrine stands at 3.6 meters high and 9.9 meters long, making it the largest shrine on Feilai Feng.
Most of the nearly 100 carvings produced during the Yuan Dynasty are located on the southern bank of Lengquan Stream and on the cliff near Qinglin Grotto and Yuru Grotto. The carvings from this period resembles the art styles of the [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang]] and [[:en:Song dynasty|Song]] dynasties, while also reflecting influences from [[:en:Tibetan Buddhism|Tibetan]] and [[:en:Mongolia|Mongolia]]n art.
==Architecture== [[File:杭州 灵隐寺 - panoramio (1).jpg|thumb|250x250px|[[:en:Shanmen|Shanmen]] of the temple]] The main axis of Lingyin follows a traditional Song dynasty five-hall Chan sect structure. The main axis stretches up the Lingyin Hill. However, the five-hall axis is a recent recreation. Only the front three halls are a part of the [[:en:Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]] axis.
===Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings=== The formal entrance of the temple is the [[:en:Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings|Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings]]. This hall is a double-eaved building. The front of the building carries a plaque ({{zh|p=Yúnlín Chán Sì|l=[[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan]] temple of the Clouds and Forests|labels=no|t=雲林禪寺}}), written by the [[:en:Kangxi Emperor|Kangxi Emperor]]. The principal statue in this hall is that of the [[Maitreya]] Buddha in his manifestation as [[:en:Budai|Budai]], or the [[:en:Laughing Buddha|Laughing Buddha]]. At the back, facing up the hill, is the [[:en:Skanda (Buddhism)|Skanda]] Buddha, or Weituo as he is known in Chinese. This statue dates from the [[:en:Southern Song Dynasty|Southern Song Dynasty]]. Being 800 years old this is the oldest and most important statue in the temple. Arranged along the left and right are the [[Four Heavenly Kings]]. The ceiling is ornately painted and decorated with [[:en:Fenghuang|phoenixes]] and [[:en:Chinese dragon|dragons]].{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=86}}
The statues of [[Four Heavenly Kings]] are imposing. Visitors to the temple are often impressed by the size and majesty of the entrance hall and its statues of the heavenly kings. Indeed, the hall of the Heavenly Kings at the Lingyin Temple is as large or larger than the main hall at many temples, reflecting its status as the center of Buddhism in Southern China.
The Hall of the Heavenly Kings is the formal entrance to the temple. However, this entry has been closed in recent years, with visitors funneled instead through side doors, where separate ticket offices are set up for admission to the temple.
===Mahavira Hall=== [[File:Hangzhou Lingyin-Temple 20161003.jpg|thumb|248x248px|The [[:en:Mahavira Hall|Mahavira Hall]]]] The second and principal hall is the [[:en:Mahavira Hall|Mahavira Hall]] (also referred to as the Grand Hall of the Great Sage). It is separated from the Hall of the Heavenly Kings by a large courtyard, featuring a raised lawn bordered with trees. To the left of the courtyard stands the [[#Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]]. The Mahavira Hall stands at 33.6 meters tall and has a roof that is triple-eaved. The interior of the hall reaches about 30 meters, with a gold-painted ceiling featuring bas-relief images of traditional Buddhist symbols.{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=86–87}}
[[File:Lingyin Buddha.JPG|thumb|The [[Shakyamuni Tathāgata]] Buddha statue at the [[:en:Mahavira Hall|Mahavira Hall]].]] The main statue enshrined within this hall is one of [[Shakyamuni Tathāgata|Sakyamuni]], the historical [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]], with his right hand forming the [[:en:Vitarka Mudrā|vitarka mudrā]]. The present statue was carved in 1956 from [[:en:Camphor|Camphor]] wood in [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang dynasty]] style and coated with 60 [[:en:Tael|Tael]]s of gold. At 24.6 meters high (including the throne on which the statue sits), it is the largest wooden Buddhist statue in China. Arranged along each side of the hall are statues of the [[:en:Twenty-Four Protective Deities|Twenty-Four protective deities]] of Chinese Buddhism, their hands carrying various Buddhist instruments of salvation as well as weapons. Statues of the [[:en:Eighteen Arhats|Eighteen arhats]] and other prominent Buddhist figures, such as the Bodhisattva [[:en:Cundi (Buddhism)|Cundi]], line the walls of the hall as well.
Behind the hall are twelve statues of various different bodhisattvas lining each wall, with six of each side. The statues include those of [[Manjushri|Manjusri]], [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]], [[Maitreya]] and [[Vajragarbha]].
, a manifestation of the Bodhisattva [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Avalokiteśvara]], at the back of the Mahavira Hall|273x273px]] At the rear wall of the hall is a [[:en:panorama|panorama]] depicting the penultimate chapter of the [[:en:Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra]], centering on [[:en:Sudhana|Sudhana]] ({{zh|t=善財童子|p=Shàncáitóngzǐ}}). In the chapter, Sudhana, in pursuit of enlightenment, goes on a pilgrimage to 53 different spiritual teachers (ranging from non-Buddhists to Bhikkhunīs to kings to devas to Bodhisattvas). The central statue of the panorama is one of the Bodhisattva [[Kannon|Guanyin]] (one of the 53 teachers). Statues of Sudhana and [[:en:en:Longnü|en:Longnü]] stand at both sides of this statue. The rest of the panorama behind the three main statues consists of more than 150 clay sculptures depicting the other spiritual teachers of Sudhana as well as other Buddhist figures such the main characters of [[:en:Journey to the West|Journey to the West]], the [[Four Heavenly Kings]] and [[:en:Ji Gong|Ji Gong]]. Figures of the Bodhisattva [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Ksitigarbha]] and [[Shakyamuni Tathāgata|Sakyamuni]] Buddha (depicting his cultivation prior to becoming the Buddha) are also incorporated into the top and middle portions of the panorama respectively.
===Hall of Bhaisajyaguru=== Further uphill and behind the main hall is the [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Hall of Bhaisajyaguru]] ({{zh|p=Yàoshī Diàn|labels=no|t=藥師殿}}), housing a statue of the [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Bhaisajyaguru]] Buddha, commonly called the Medicine Buddha. Statues of the Bodhisattvas [[:en:Sūryaprabha|Sūryaprabha]] and [[:en:Candraprabha|Candraprabha]], who are traditionally regarded as the attendants of Bhaisajyaguru, stand on the left and right side of Bhaisajyaguru's statue respectively.
Twelve statues of the [[Twelve Heavenly Generals]], who are protective [[:en:Yaksha|Yaksha]] attendants of [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Bhaisajyaguru]], stand on both sides of the Hall of Bhaisajyaguru, with 6 situated on each side. The names of each General along with their associated iconography are: Kumbhira (armed with a yellow vajra), Vajra (armed with a white sword), Mihira (armed with a yellow vajra), Andira (armed with a green mallet), Anila (armed with a red trident), Sandila (armed with a black sword), Indra (armed with a red staff or halberd), Pajra (armed with a red mallet), Makura (armed with a white ax), Kinnara (armed with a yellow rope), Catura (armed with a green mallet), and Vikarala (armed with a red three-pointed vajra).
=== Hall of Ji Gong === [[File:Lingyin Temple, 2020-11-29 16.jpg|thumb|246x246px|The Hall of [[:en:Ji Gong|Ji Gong]]]] This hall is situated to the east of the Hall of Bhaisajyaguru and enshrines a statue of the Song dynasty monk [[:en:Ji Gong|Ji Gong]] (also known as "Daoji"). The statue is made of bronze, with a height of 2.3 meters and a weight of 2.5 tons. The right hand of the statue holds a broken fan, the left hand carries Buddhist prayer beads, and the right foot is shown dipping into a wine jar. Eighteen huge murals depicting a narration of Ji Gong’s life are painted on the walls at both sides of the hall. Each mural is 3 meters high and 3 meters long, with the entire display being 50 meter long.
===Dharma Hall=== [[File:Hangzhou-Lingyin-Tempel-52-Teich-Pavillons-2012-gje.jpg|thumb|249x249px|[[:en:Free Life Pond|Free Life Pond]] of the temple]] The [[:en:Dharma Hall|Dharma Hall]] is located behind the Hall of Bhaisajyaguru and is the main place where the Buddhist sutras are expounded by the resident monastics. The present Dharma Hall building was constructed by a monk from the temple named Xuanli in 1446.
=== Cultural Relics Exhibition Hall === The Cultural Relics Exhibition Hall lies on the basement floor of the Dharma Hall and displays the collection of Buddhist cultural relics maintained by the temple.
The hall covers a total area of 638 square meters and is installed with waterproof, fireproof, damp-proof, electronic surveillance and air-conditioning systems. It houses an exhibition of over 40 showcases with collections of cultural relics that have been treasured by the temple for many years. These cultural relics are categorized by the temple into four categories: first, Buddhist ritual implements used by successive abbots of Lingyin Temple, such as horsetail whisks and [[:en:Ruyi (scepter)|ruyi scepters]]; second, common antiques such as porcelain vases from the Southern Song Dynasty; third, Buddhist antiques such as sutras written by Tang dynasty Chinese Buddhists and unearthed Buddhist statues; fourth, ancient paintings and calligraphy, such as calligraphy scrolls in seal characters by [[:en:Wu Changshuo|Wu Changshuo]], fan paintings by [[:en:Ren Bonian|Ren Bonian]] and couplets by [[:en:Sha Menghai|Sha Menghai]].
=== Buddhist Texts Library === Uphill from the Hall of the Medicine Buddha is the [[:en:Buddhist Texts Library|Buddhist Texts Library]]. This, and the Huayan Hall behind it, were built from 2000 to 2002 to recreate the five-hall main axis. The Sutra Library does not house a major statue and is not open for worship.
===Huayan Hall=== The fifth and last hall on the main axis is the Avatamsaka Hall, or Huayan Hall ({{zh|c=华严殿|p=Huáyán Diàn|labels=no}}). Also built in 2002, this hall houses statues of the three sages of the [[:en:Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra]], known as the Huayan Sutra in [[:en:Chinese language|Chinese]] – [[Shakyamuni Tathāgata|Sakyamuni]], [[:en:Manjusri|Manjusri]], and [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]].
A 3 meter high bronze statue of the Japanese Buddhist monk [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]], who traveled to China during the Tang Dynasty to study [[:en:Chinese Esoteric Buddhism|Chinese Esoteric Buddhism]] and who visited Lingyin Temple during his travels, stands in a bamboo grove between the Dharma Hall and the Huayan Hall. The statue portrays Kūkai in monastic robes, holding Buddhist prayer beads in his left hand, and a walking stick in his right hand. The statue was erected in 2002 as a symbol of the friendship between Buddhist circles in both China and Japan.
===Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats=== The Hall of Five Hundred Arhats ({{zh|t=五百羅漢堂|p=Wǔbǎi Luóhàn Táng|labels=no}}), also a modern addition, faces onto the western side of the courtyard in front of the main hall. The building has a complex floor plan, shaped like a Buddhist [[:en:Swastika|Swastika]]. Bronze statues of the five hundred arhats are arranged along the arms of the swastika, with each statue seated on a unique ornate seat. Each statue measures 1.7 meters in height, 1.3 meters in width, and weighs around 1 ton.
At the center of the hall, where the arms of the swastika join, stands a bronze canopy housing statues of the four main bodhisattvas in Chinese Buddhism: [[Kannon|Guanyin]], [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Ksitigarbha]], [[Manjushri|Manjusri]] and [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]], who represent the four cardinal directions. This canopy is 12.62 meters in height, 7.77 meters wide and occupies 5 square meters. It is currently the tallest solid bronze structure in the world.
=== Two Sutra Pillars === The two sutra pillars are located in the eastern and western sides of the Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings. The eastern pillar stands at 7.17 meters high and the western pillar stands at 11 meters high. Both pillars are engraved with the [[:en:Uṣṇīṣa Vijaya Dhāraṇī Sūtra|Uṣṇīṣa Vijaya Dhāraṇī Sūtra]], as well as reliefs of various Buddhist figures and tales. Both pillars were built in the year 969 in the state of [[:en:Wuyue|Wuyue]] during the end of the [[:en:Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period|Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period]] and the beginning of the [[:en:Song dynasty|Song Dynasty]] and were moved to their present location in the temple in the year 1053.
==Notable monks== *[[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]] - An Indian monk who founded the temple *[[:en:Ji Gong|Daoji]] – A saintly Buddhist monk who is highly venerated in [[:en:Chinese folk religion|Chinese folk religion]] and popularly known as "Ji Gong". *Dachuan Lingyin Puji (1179–1253)- compiler of the Wudeng Huiyan (''Compendium of Five Lamps'')

{{Infobox Buddhist temple|image=File:Lingyin si.JPG|prefecture={{ill|Xihu District|qid=Q155441}}|coordinates={{Coord|30.24277778|N|120.09666667|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q1070228]] Wikidata name: Lingyin Temple [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:51, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Use American English|date=April 2023}} {{Use mdy dates|date=April 2023}} {{Short description|Buddhist temple in Hangzhou, China}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Lingyin temple | native_name = 灵隐寺 | native_name_lang = zh | image = Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou 20161003.jpg | caption = [[:en:Hall of Bhaisajyaguru|Hall of Bhaisajyaguru]] in the Temple | map_type = Zhejiang#China | map_caption = | coordinates = {{coord|30.2427777778|N|120.096666667|E|type:landmark_region:China|format=dms|display=title,inline}} | coordinates_footnotes = | religious_affiliation = [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] | sect = [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhism]] | leadership = Shi Guangquan ({{zh|s=释光泉|t=|labels=no}}) | festival = | location = [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]], [[:en:Zhejiang|Zhejiang]] | country = China | consecration_year = | website = {{URL|http://www.lingyinsi.org/}} | architect = | architecture_type = | architecture_style = [[:en:Chinese architecture|Chinese architecture]] | founded_by = [[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]] | creator = | funded_by = | general_contractor = | established = 328 | groundbreaking = | year_completed = [[:en:Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]] (reconstruction) | construction_cost = | date_demolished = | footnotes = }} [[File:West Lake Map.png|thumb|Map of the West Lake in Hangzhou, China, with the location of Lingyin Temple]] [[File:Chanting at Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou.ogg|thumb|Buddhist monks chanting at Lingyin Temple, [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]], October 2010.]]
'''Lingyin Temple''' ({{zh|t=靈隱寺|s=灵隐寺|p=Língyǐn Sì}}) is a prominent [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhist]] temple near [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]] that is renowned for its many pagodas and grottos.{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=85}} Its name is commonly and literally translated into English as '''Temple of the Soul's Retreat'''.
The monastery is the largest of several temples in the Wulin Mountains ({{zh|c=武林山|p=Wǔlínshān}}), which feature renowned grottos and religious rock carvings.
==History== According to tradition, the monastery was founded in 328 AD during the [[:en:Eastern Jin dynasty|Eastern Jin dynasty]] (266–420) by an Indian monk, named [[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]] in Chinese. From its inception, Lingyin was a famous monastery in the [[:en:Jiangnan|Jiangnan]] region.{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=85}} At its peak under the [[:en:Wuyue|Wuyue]] Kingdom (907–978), the temple boasted 18 pavilions, 72 halls, more than 1300 dormitory rooms, inhabited by more than 3000 monks. Many of the rich Buddhist carvings in the Feilai Feng grottos and surrounding mountains also date from this era.
During the [[:en:Southern Song Dynasty|Southern Song]] (1127–1279), the monastery was regarded as one of the ten most important temples of the Chan sect in the [[:en:Jiangnan|Jiangnan]] region. However, its prominence has not saved the temple from marauders. It has been rebuilt no less than sixteen times since then. While certain existing buildings date from previous Chinese dynasties, much of the current buildings are modern restorations from the late [[:en:Qing dynasty|Qing]] (1644–1911) period.
During the [[:en:Cultural Revolution|Cultural Revolution]], the temple and grounds suffered damage at the hands of [[:en:Red Guards (China)|red guards]], but the students of [[:en:Zhejiang University|Zhejiang University]] tried to protect the temple. The temple managed to avoid large scale destruction partly because of the instructions of Premier [[:en:Zhou Enlai|Zhou Enlai]].
Today the temple is thriving as a destination for both pilgrims and tourists. It is regarded as one of the wealthiest monasteries in China, and regular pilgrims have included former paramount leader [[:en:Deng Xiaoping|Deng Xiaoping]].
==Surroundings== The Wuling Mountains are a renowned site for [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan Buddhism]] in Southern China. A number of smaller temples are also located in the area. Today, Lingyin and the surrounding areas are marketed as the Lingyin-Feilai Feng Scenic Area, with ticketed admission. Visitors enter from a screen wall marked with a four character inscription "the Western Heaven is within reach" ({{zh|t=咫尺西天|p=zhíchǐ Xītiān|l=Western Heaven is between 0.8 and one foot away|labels=no}}). Proceeding down the road from the entrance, the visitor first sees Feilai Feng on the left, then Lingyin Hill on the right. The entire scenic area is dotted with historic buildings and artwork, including pagodas, pavilions, bridges, and statues. The largest stone pagoda is located near the entrance. Called Elder Li's Pagoda ({{zh|t=理公塔}}), it houses the ashes of Huili. The area is thickly wooded.
==Feilai Feng grottos== [[File:LigongPagoda.jpg|thumb|left|Pagoda containing [[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]]'s ashes at the foot of Feilai Feng.|300x300px]] [[File:Lingyin grotto.JPG|thumb|right|[[:en:Rock reliefs|Rock reliefs]] at Feilai Feng; the panel at lower left depicts the pilgrims of the ''[[:en:Journey to the West|Journey to the West]]''|188x188px]] [[File:Maitreya and disciples carving in Feilai Feng Caves.jpg|thumb|Relief of [[:en:Budai|Budai]] as [[Maitreya]], with disciples]] Feilai Feng, or "the Peak that Flew Hither", also commonly translated as "Flying Peak" ([[:en:Traditional Chinese characters|Traditional Chinese]]: 飛來峰石窟; [[:en:Simplified Chinese characters|Simplified Chinese]]:飞来峰石窟), is located in front of the temple proper. The peak is so-named because it is made of limestone, giving it a craggy appearance very different from the surrounding mountains. Legend holds that the peak was originally from [[:en:India|India]] (with some versions suggesting that it is [[:en:Vulture Peak|Vulture Peak]]), but flew to [[:en:Hangzhou|Hangzhou]] overnight as a demonstration of the omnipotence of Buddhist law. Many grottos can be found on the peak, such as Qinglin Grotto, Yuru Grotto and Longhong Grotto. Many [[:en:rock relief|rock relief]]s dot the peak surface, and more are located in the various caves and grottos throughout the peak. Within the main cave, dedicated to the [[:en:Bodhisattva|Bodhisattva]] [[Kannon|Guanyin]], there is a crack in the ceiling of the cave that stretches up to the surface, so that a person standing at a certain position can see a sliver of sunlight. This is known as the "one thread of heaven" ([[:en:Traditional Chinese characters|Traditional Chinese]]: 一線天; [[:en:Simplified Chinese characters|Simplified Chinese]]: 一线天; [[:en:Pinyin|Pinyin]]: ''Yīxiàn Tiān'').{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=86–87}}
The stone carvings on Feilai Feng are located in an area measuring 600 meters long and 200 meters wide. In total, there are 153 shrines and more than 470 pieces of carvings, among which 338 are relatively well-preserved, 96 carvings from the [[:en:Yuan dynasty|Yuan Dynasty]] as well as several from the [[:en:Ming dynasty|Ming Dynasty]].
Around 11 carvings date to the late [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang Dynasty]] and [[:en:Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period|Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period]]. These carvings dot the top of the peak and the mouth of Qinglin Grotto and they all prominently feature the “Three Saints of the West”, which refers to the triad of [[Amitābha]] Buddha and the Bodhisattvas [[Kannon|Guanyin]] and [[:en:Mahasthamaprapta|Mahasthamaprapta]] from [[:en:Pure Land Buddhism|Pure Land Buddhism]].
A total of 222 carvings were produced in the [[:en:Song dynasty|Northern Song Dynasty]] period, which feature a diverse range of Buddhist figures including the Six Patriarchs of [[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan]] (or [[:en:Zen|Zen]]) Buddhism, various arhats, Bodhisattvas and Buddhas such as [[:en:Vairocana|Vairocana]]. One of the more prominent carvings from this period is a shrine to [[:en:Budai|Budai]], a monk who is traditionally regarded as an incarnation of [[Maitreya]], surrounded by the [[:en:Eighteen Arhats|Eighteen Arhats]]. This shrine stands at 3.6 meters high and 9.9 meters long, making it the largest shrine on Feilai Feng.
Most of the nearly 100 carvings produced during the Yuan Dynasty are located on the southern bank of Lengquan Stream and on the cliff near Qinglin Grotto and Yuru Grotto. The carvings from this period resembles the art styles of the [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang]] and [[:en:Song dynasty|Song]] dynasties, while also reflecting influences from [[:en:Tibetan Buddhism|Tibetan]] and [[:en:Mongolia|Mongolia]]n art.
==Architecture== [[File:杭州 灵隐寺 - panoramio (1).jpg|thumb|250x250px|[[:en:Shanmen|Shanmen]] of the temple]] The main axis of Lingyin follows a traditional Song dynasty five-hall Chan sect structure. The main axis stretches up the Lingyin Hill. However, the five-hall axis is a recent recreation. Only the front three halls are a part of the [[:en:Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]] axis.
===Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings=== The formal entrance of the temple is the [[:en:Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings|Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings]]. This hall is a double-eaved building. The front of the building carries a plaque ({{zh|p=Yúnlín Chán Sì|l=[[:en:Chan Buddhism|Chan]] temple of the Clouds and Forests|labels=no|t=雲林禪寺}}), written by the [[:en:Kangxi Emperor|Kangxi Emperor]]. The principal statue in this hall is that of the [[Maitreya]] Buddha in his manifestation as [[:en:Budai|Budai]], or the [[:en:Laughing Buddha|Laughing Buddha]]. At the back, facing up the hill, is the [[:en:Skanda (Buddhism)|Skanda]] Buddha, or Weituo as he is known in Chinese. This statue dates from the [[:en:Southern Song Dynasty|Southern Song Dynasty]]. Being 800 years old this is the oldest and most important statue in the temple. Arranged along the left and right are the [[Four Heavenly Kings]]. The ceiling is ornately painted and decorated with [[:en:Fenghuang|phoenixes]] and [[:en:Chinese dragon|dragons]].{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=86}}
The statues of [[Four Heavenly Kings]] are imposing. Visitors to the temple are often impressed by the size and majesty of the entrance hall and its statues of the heavenly kings. Indeed, the hall of the Heavenly Kings at the Lingyin Temple is as large or larger than the main hall at many temples, reflecting its status as the center of Buddhism in Southern China.
The Hall of the Heavenly Kings is the formal entrance to the temple. However, this entry has been closed in recent years, with visitors funneled instead through side doors, where separate ticket offices are set up for admission to the temple.
===Mahavira Hall=== [[File:Hangzhou Lingyin-Temple 20161003.jpg|thumb|248x248px|The [[:en:Mahavira Hall|Mahavira Hall]]]] The second and principal hall is the [[:en:Mahavira Hall|Mahavira Hall]] (also referred to as the Grand Hall of the Great Sage). It is separated from the Hall of the Heavenly Kings by a large courtyard, featuring a raised lawn bordered with trees. To the left of the courtyard stands the [[#Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]]. The Mahavira Hall stands at 33.6 meters tall and has a roof that is triple-eaved. The interior of the hall reaches about 30 meters, with a gold-painted ceiling featuring bas-relief images of traditional Buddhist symbols.{{sfnb|Zi Yan|2012|p=86–87}}
[[File:Lingyin Buddha.JPG|thumb|The [[Shakyamuni Tathāgata]] Buddha statue at the [[:en:Mahavira Hall|Mahavira Hall]].]] The main statue enshrined within this hall is one of [[Shakyamuni Tathāgata|Sakyamuni]], the historical [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]], with his right hand forming the [[:en:Vitarka Mudrā|vitarka mudrā]]. The present statue was carved in 1956 from [[:en:Camphor|Camphor]] wood in [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang dynasty]] style and coated with 60 [[:en:Tael|Tael]]s of gold. At 24.6 meters high (including the throne on which the statue sits), it is the largest wooden Buddhist statue in China. Arranged along each side of the hall are statues of the [[:en:Twenty-Four Protective Deities|Twenty-Four protective deities]] of Chinese Buddhism, their hands carrying various Buddhist instruments of salvation as well as weapons. Statues of the [[:en:Eighteen Arhats|Eighteen arhats]] and other prominent Buddhist figures, such as the Bodhisattva [[:en:Cundi (Buddhism)|Cundi]], line the walls of the hall as well.
Behind the hall are twelve statues of various different bodhisattvas lining each wall, with six of each side. The statues include those of [[Manjushri|Manjusri]], [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]], [[Maitreya]] and [[Vajragarbha]].
, a manifestation of the Bodhisattva [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Avalokiteśvara]], at the back of the Mahavira Hall|273x273px]] At the rear wall of the hall is a [[:en:panorama|panorama]] depicting the penultimate chapter of the [[:en:Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra]], centering on [[:en:Sudhana|Sudhana]] ({{zh|t=善財童子|p=Shàncáitóngzǐ}}). In the chapter, Sudhana, in pursuit of enlightenment, goes on a pilgrimage to 53 different spiritual teachers (ranging from non-Buddhists to Bhikkhunīs to kings to devas to Bodhisattvas). The central statue of the panorama is one of the Bodhisattva [[Kannon|Guanyin]] (one of the 53 teachers). Statues of Sudhana and [[:en:en:Longnü|en:Longnü]] stand at both sides of this statue. The rest of the panorama behind the three main statues consists of more than 150 clay sculptures depicting the other spiritual teachers of Sudhana as well as other Buddhist figures such the main characters of [[:en:Journey to the West|Journey to the West]], the [[Four Heavenly Kings]] and [[:en:Ji Gong|Ji Gong]]. Figures of the Bodhisattva [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Ksitigarbha]] and [[Shakyamuni Tathāgata|Sakyamuni]] Buddha (depicting his cultivation prior to becoming the Buddha) are also incorporated into the top and middle portions of the panorama respectively.
===Hall of Bhaisajyaguru=== Further uphill and behind the main hall is the [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Hall of Bhaisajyaguru]] ({{zh|p=Yàoshī Diàn|labels=no|t=藥師殿}}), housing a statue of the [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Bhaisajyaguru]] Buddha, commonly called the Medicine Buddha. Statues of the Bodhisattvas [[:en:Sūryaprabha|Sūryaprabha]] and [[:en:Candraprabha|Candraprabha]], who are traditionally regarded as the attendants of Bhaisajyaguru, stand on the left and right side of Bhaisajyaguru's statue respectively.
Twelve statues of the [[Twelve Heavenly Generals]], who are protective [[:en:Yaksha|Yaksha]] attendants of [[:en:Bhaisajyaguru|Bhaisajyaguru]], stand on both sides of the Hall of Bhaisajyaguru, with 6 situated on each side. The names of each General along with their associated iconography are: Kumbhira (armed with a yellow vajra), Vajra (armed with a white sword), Mihira (armed with a yellow vajra), Andira (armed with a green mallet), Anila (armed with a red trident), Sandila (armed with a black sword), Indra (armed with a red staff or halberd), Pajra (armed with a red mallet), Makura (armed with a white ax), Kinnara (armed with a yellow rope), Catura (armed with a green mallet), and Vikarala (armed with a red three-pointed vajra).
=== Hall of Ji Gong === [[File:Lingyin Temple, 2020-11-29 16.jpg|thumb|246x246px|The Hall of [[:en:Ji Gong|Ji Gong]]]] This hall is situated to the east of the Hall of Bhaisajyaguru and enshrines a statue of the Song dynasty monk [[:en:Ji Gong|Ji Gong]] (also known as "Daoji"). The statue is made of bronze, with a height of 2.3 meters and a weight of 2.5 tons. The right hand of the statue holds a broken fan, the left hand carries Buddhist prayer beads, and the right foot is shown dipping into a wine jar. Eighteen huge murals depicting a narration of Ji Gong’s life are painted on the walls at both sides of the hall. Each mural is 3 meters high and 3 meters long, with the entire display being 50 meter long.
===Dharma Hall=== [[File:Hangzhou-Lingyin-Tempel-52-Teich-Pavillons-2012-gje.jpg|thumb|249x249px|[[:en:Free Life Pond|Free Life Pond]] of the temple]] The [[:en:Dharma Hall|Dharma Hall]] is located behind the Hall of Bhaisajyaguru and is the main place where the Buddhist sutras are expounded by the resident monastics. The present Dharma Hall building was constructed by a monk from the temple named Xuanli in 1446.
=== Cultural Relics Exhibition Hall === The Cultural Relics Exhibition Hall lies on the basement floor of the Dharma Hall and displays the collection of Buddhist cultural relics maintained by the temple.
The hall covers a total area of 638 square meters and is installed with waterproof, fireproof, damp-proof, electronic surveillance and air-conditioning systems. It houses an exhibition of over 40 showcases with collections of cultural relics that have been treasured by the temple for many years. These cultural relics are categorized by the temple into four categories: first, Buddhist ritual implements used by successive abbots of Lingyin Temple, such as horsetail whisks and [[:en:Ruyi (scepter)|ruyi scepters]]; second, common antiques such as porcelain vases from the Southern Song Dynasty; third, Buddhist antiques such as sutras written by Tang dynasty Chinese Buddhists and unearthed Buddhist statues; fourth, ancient paintings and calligraphy, such as calligraphy scrolls in seal characters by [[:en:Wu Changshuo|Wu Changshuo]], fan paintings by [[:en:Ren Bonian|Ren Bonian]] and couplets by [[:en:Sha Menghai|Sha Menghai]].
=== Buddhist Texts Library === Uphill from the Hall of the Medicine Buddha is the [[:en:Buddhist Texts Library|Buddhist Texts Library]]. This, and the Huayan Hall behind it, were built from 2000 to 2002 to recreate the five-hall main axis. The Sutra Library does not house a major statue and is not open for worship.
===Huayan Hall=== The fifth and last hall on the main axis is the Avatamsaka Hall, or Huayan Hall ({{zh|c=华严殿|p=Huáyán Diàn|labels=no}}). Also built in 2002, this hall houses statues of the three sages of the [[:en:Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra]], known as the Huayan Sutra in [[:en:Chinese language|Chinese]] – [[Shakyamuni Tathāgata|Sakyamuni]], [[:en:Manjusri|Manjusri]], and [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]].
A 3 meter high bronze statue of the Japanese Buddhist monk [[:en:Kūkai|Kūkai]], who traveled to China during the Tang Dynasty to study [[:en:Chinese Esoteric Buddhism|Chinese Esoteric Buddhism]] and who visited Lingyin Temple during his travels, stands in a bamboo grove between the Dharma Hall and the Huayan Hall. The statue portrays Kūkai in monastic robes, holding Buddhist prayer beads in his left hand, and a walking stick in his right hand. The statue was erected in 2002 as a symbol of the friendship between Buddhist circles in both China and Japan.
===Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats=== The Hall of Five Hundred Arhats ({{zh|t=五百羅漢堂|p=Wǔbǎi Luóhàn Táng|labels=no}}), also a modern addition, faces onto the western side of the courtyard in front of the main hall. The building has a complex floor plan, shaped like a Buddhist [[:en:Swastika|Swastika]]. Bronze statues of the five hundred arhats are arranged along the arms of the swastika, with each statue seated on a unique ornate seat. Each statue measures 1.7 meters in height, 1.3 meters in width, and weighs around 1 ton.
At the center of the hall, where the arms of the swastika join, stands a bronze canopy housing statues of the four main bodhisattvas in Chinese Buddhism: [[Kannon|Guanyin]], [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Ksitigarbha]], [[Manjushri|Manjusri]] and [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]], who represent the four cardinal directions. This canopy is 12.62 meters in height, 7.77 meters wide and occupies 5 square meters. It is currently the tallest solid bronze structure in the world.
=== Two Sutra Pillars === The two sutra pillars are located in the eastern and western sides of the Hall of the Four Heavenly Kings. The eastern pillar stands at 7.17 meters high and the western pillar stands at 11 meters high. Both pillars are engraved with the [[:en:Uṣṇīṣa Vijaya Dhāraṇī Sūtra|Uṣṇīṣa Vijaya Dhāraṇī Sūtra]], as well as reliefs of various Buddhist figures and tales. Both pillars were built in the year 969 in the state of [[:en:Wuyue|Wuyue]] during the end of the [[:en:Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period|Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms Period]] and the beginning of the [[:en:Song dynasty|Song Dynasty]] and were moved to their present location in the temple in the year 1053.
==Notable monks== *[[:en:Huili (monk)|Huili]] - An Indian monk who founded the temple *[[:en:Ji Gong|Daoji]] – A saintly Buddhist monk who is highly venerated in [[:en:Chinese folk religion|Chinese folk religion]] and popularly known as "Ji Gong". *Dachuan Lingyin Puji (1179–1253)- compiler of the Wudeng Huiyan (''Compendium of Five Lamps'')

Hangzhou, China Part 1.jpg|Statues of the [[:en:Twenty-Four Protective Deities|Twenty-Four Devas]] (二十四諸天 ''Èrshísì Zhūtiān'') on the right side of the Mahavira Hall File:Xihu, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China - panoramio (32).jpg|Arhat statues enshrined inside the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:杭州.灵隐寺（五百罗汉堂） - panoramio (1).jpg|Statue of [[Manjushri|Manjusri]] in the Bronze Canopy within the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:杭州.灵隐寺（五百罗汉堂） - panoramio (2).jpg|Statue of [[Kannon|Guanyin]] in the Bronze Canopy within the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:杭州.灵隐寺（五百罗汉堂） - panoramio (3).jpg|Statue of [[:en:Kṣitigarbha|Ksitigarbha]] in the Bronze Canopy within the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:杭州.灵隐寺（五百罗汉堂） - panoramio (4).jpg|Statue of [[:en:Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|Samantabhadra]] in the Bronze Canopy within the [[:en:Arhat Hall|Hall of the Five Hundred Arhats]] File:2013.1灵隐0154.JPG|Rock carving of [[:en:Budai|Budai]] in the grottos File:Lingyin Temple 20150623 100717.jpg|Statues in the grottos File:Lingyin temple 03.jpg|Statues in the grottos File:Hangzhou-Lingyin-Tempel-60-Buddha-Grotten-2012-gje.jpg|Statues in the grottos </gallery>
